sections.heading: Seeing life from the edge of eternity
sections.text: Lord, when I pray, you draw me out beyond the smallness of this present life. I begin to see the world differently. The things that usually impress me, distract me, or crush me lose their weight. The pleasures that promise so much and the disappointments that hurt so deeply are not ultimate. In your presence, I remember that I am small, that you are eternal, and that my life only makes sense when it is lived for you.
theological_themes: Prayer brings the believer into conscious fellowship with the eternal God.
Eternal perspective relativizes earthly pleasures, disappointments, and fears.
Humility grows when the soul sees God as he is.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts visible, temporary afflictions with unseen eternal glory. This supports the prayer’s movement from the pressures of mortal life into a God-given eternal perspective.
Believers are called to set their minds on things above because their life is hidden with Christ. This grounds the prayer’s desire to see ordinary life in light of eternity.

sections.heading: Being carried by the Spirit toward home
sections.text: Thank you for the Holy Spirit, who carries me when I do not have strength in myself. Let him fill my praying with fresh longing for you. Keep moving me toward the city you have promised, where your people will live with you forever. Make my heart thirsty to belong to you more fully, not just in words, but with my whole life.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit helps and strengthens believers in prayer.
The Christian life is pilgrimage toward the heavenly city.
True prayer awakens longing for deeper holiness and fuller communion with God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes according to God’s will. This directly supports the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit in prayer.
Hebrews describes believers as having come to the heavenly Jerusalem through Christ. This illuminates the prayer’s hope of being carried toward the promised city of God.

sections.heading: Letting lesser things fall away
sections.text: When I am with you in prayer, the things below stop looking so large. What matters most becomes clearer: a heart made holy before you, and people brought safely to Christ. My worries, fears, and anxious thoughts shrink in your hands. They are real, but they are not lord over me. You are.
theological_themes: Prayer reorders loves and priorities around holiness and salvation.
God’s presence gives peace that displaces anxiety.
Earthly cares are brought under God’s rule rather than denied.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells believers to bring anxieties to God in prayer, with the promise of God’s peace guarding them. This supports the section’s movement from fear and care into trustful prayer.
Jesus teaches his disciples not to be ruled by anxious concern, but to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness first. This fits the prayer’s shift from worldly concerns to holiness and salvation.

sections.heading: Rejoicing in what you are doing in your church
sections.text: Father, give me joy in what you are doing among your people. Make me glad when your church is built up, when sinners come home to you, and when your name becomes great because of mercy shown to people who did not deserve it. Let me care more about your kingdom than my reputation, comfort, or success.
theological_themes: God glorifies his name by saving sinners and gathering them to himself.
The believer’s joy is enlarged by God’s work in the church.
Prayer aligns personal desires with the coming of God’s kingdom.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. This grounds the prayer’s joy and longing over sinners returning to God.
Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for God’s name to be honored and his kingdom to come. This supports the section’s desire that God’s name be made great through his saving work.

sections.heading: Putting myself and my concerns in your hands
sections.text: In prayer, lift me above both criticism and praise. Let neither people’s rejection nor their approval control me. Give me a taste of the joy that belongs to your kingdom, so that I can hand myself over to you without holding anything back. I place my concerns, plans, desires, and future in your hands. Do with me what is right and good. I do not want to live as if my will were the center of everything. I want to be yours, completely and forever.
theological_themes: Prayer frees believers from bondage to human approval.
Surrender means entrusting the whole self and future to God’s wise will.
Heavenly joy strengthens wholehearted devotion to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts seeking human approval with being a servant of Christ. This supports the prayer’s desire to be lifted above both flattery and disapproval.
Paul calls believers to offer themselves to God as living sacrifices and be transformed in mind. This grounds the prayer’s language of placing the whole self at God’s disposal.

sections.heading: Praying freely for others as your child
sections.text: Father, teach me to pray freely for others: for my friends, for those who lead and serve your church, for people who do not yet know you, for your whole church, and for your kingdom to come in this world. Let me come to you honestly and warmly, as your child speaking to a good Father, with deep affection for you and real hope in what you can do.
theological_themes: Believers are invited to intercede broadly for others.
Christian prayer is both reverent and intimate because God is Father.
Hopeful intercession rests on God’s saving desire and kingdom purposes.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges prayers and intercessions for all kinds of people and connects this with God’s saving purposes. This supports praying for friends, leaders, sinners, and the wider world.
Believers receive the Spirit of adoption and cry to God as Father. This grounds the section’s confidence and openness before God as his child.

sections.heading: Making my life prayerful
sections.text: Lord, do not let prayer be only something I visit and then leave behind. Make me a person who keeps turning toward you. Teach me to pray in the middle of ordinary life, to depend on you without stopping, and to live each day in steady conversation with you.
theological_themes: Prayer is not only an activity but a continuing posture of dependence on God.
Believers are called to persistent prayer in all circumstances.
A life of prayer expresses ongoing communion with God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers to pray without ceasing and give thanks in all circumstances. This directly supports the prayer’s final request to become continually prayerful.
Paul calls believers to pray at all times in the Spirit with perseverance for all the saints. This supports both continual prayer and intercession for the church.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about entering the eternal world in prayer could be misunderstood as mystical escape from embodied life. I rendered it as God-given eternal perspective and communion with God, not as leaving ordinary responsibilities behind.

The original says the believer has 'no will or interest of my own.' I preserved the force of surrender while avoiding the implication that personal creaturely desires are inherently evil; the modern version frames it as refusing to make one’s own will the center.

The phrase 'as a lover to the beloved' can sound romantic in contemporary English when addressed to God. I rendered it as deep affection and warmth toward God, while keeping the original’s sense of intimate, free prayer.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated 'New Jerusalem' as the believer’s eschatological hope and pilgrimage toward God’s promised city, rather than as a vague symbol of spiritual progress.
I interpreted 'sinners returning to Zion' as repentance and conversion into the people of God, so the prayer asks for sinners to come home to God and for his name to be honored through mercy.

I kept the original’s strong contrast between eternal realities and worldly cares, but stated that earthly worries are real while not ultimate, to preserve both the Puritan intensity and biblical pastoral balance.
